title: Protective immunity that covers a viral family, including future variants and unseen relatives

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a vaccine design method that produces durable human protection across substantial viral diversity, including protection against related viruses whose exact surface proteins were not included in the vaccine. Instead of depending mainly on a close match to currently circulating strains, it would direct immunity toward vulnerable viral features that remain sufficiently similar across diverse members of the target group. Coverage of future variants and unseen relatives is the intended capability; it has not been established for every possible future virus.

One concrete route is germline targeting: designing an initial vaccine antigen to recruit rare B cells with the genetic potential to develop into broadly neutralizing antibody lineages, then using subsequent immunizations to guide their maturation. Human HIV research demonstrates that such precursor cells can be recruited and can acquire features associated with broad neutralization. The proposed advance requires completing that process into responses with enough breadth, potency and persistence to protect people. Responses against multiple conserved sites could reduce vulnerability to escape, although they would not make escape impossible.

Proposed scope: establish protective breadth for one highly variable viral target and then demonstrate that the same design logic can produce protection in a second viral family. Breadth within HIV, coverage across influenza A groups, and breadth within sarbecoviruses describe different biological scopes. Sarbecoviruses are a subgroup of coronaviruses, so a pan-sarbecovirus result would not by itself establish protection across the entire coronavirus family. Transfer to a second family would demonstrate some generality of the method, rather than universal transferability.

significance.text: Seasonal influenza vaccines are reformulated annually to match strains expected to circulate, while the retained HIV study describes an effective HIV vaccine as an unmet goal. Durable protection across antigenically diverse viruses would substantially change vaccine design by reducing dependence on close antigen matching. For a successfully demonstrated target, the direct benefit would be protection that remains useful across a wider range of circulating viruses than a narrowly matched response.

Protection against related viruses absent from a vaccine could also provide a basis for preparing before a particular relative causes a human outbreak. UW Medicine's report of such protection in animals supplies a technical foundation for that possibility. Demonstrating the same outcome in humans would be a substantial further advance; demonstrating a shared design logic across two viral families would strengthen the case for a reusable approach to vaccine development.

Limits of the projected impact: conserved-site targeting does not guarantee protection against every drifted virus, antigenic shift or unseen relative. Protection lasting one year would not establish permanent freedom from seasonal vaccination, and protection against disease would not automatically establish prevention of infection or transmission. Reduced vaccine updating, fewer outbreaks and broader preparedness are conditional downstream possibilities whose extent would depend on measured coverage, durability, escape and deployment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable induction of sufficiently broad, potent and durable protective immunity in humans despite viral antigenic diversity. The HIV work illustrates why starting a useful antibody lineage is only an initial step: most B cells lack the intrinsic genetic capacity to become broadly neutralizing antibody producers, and recruiting suitable precursors does not establish that subsequent immunizations will mature them into protective responses. The retained study identifies the ability of booster immunogens to shape those lineages as a priority.

A concrete barrier is recognition of the viral surface in its native form. In the GT1.1 study, some isolated antibodies neutralized wild-type pseudoviruses, but neutralization of a fully glycosylated tier-2 test virus was weak, and additional heterologous neutralization was especially evident for viruses naturally lacking the N276 glycan. These results show progress toward the desired antibody properties while exposing remaining limits in potency and access to glycan-shielded targets. Laboratory activity by selected antibodies also does not establish that vaccination produces protective concentrations and breadth in people.

Engineering synthesis: a successful immunization sequence would need to guide the desired lineages through maturation despite competing responses to more variable surfaces, sustain the resulting immunity, and retain activity across a demanding range of viral diversity. Combining responses to multiple conserved sites is a plausible way to reduce escape risk, but the required combination remains to be established. The supplied evidence does not establish that two or three specificities are a universal requirement or a sufficient solution.

A further barrier is translating breadth in selected laboratory assays or animal challenges into reproducible human protection. A method that works within one viral group may encounter different antigen structures, immune targets and escape routes in another. Demonstrating transfer therefore requires a second protective result with a clearly defined biological scope, rather than assuming that a successful antigen format or precursor-targeting strategy will work unchanged across families.

current_state.text: Caniels and colleagues' GT1.1 paper is dated 2025 in the document described by the supplied review, correcting the research notes' 2026 attribution. IAVI C101 was a phase 1 safety and immunogenicity trial of the germline-targeting trimer GT1.1 with AS01B. It enrolled 47 participants: 20 assigned low dose, 19 high dose and eight placebo. Detectable VRC01-class responses occurred in 11 of 18 evaluable low-dose recipients, or 61%, and 13 of 19 high-dose recipients, or 68%. Thus, the supported finding is a response in a majority of evaluable vaccine recipients, rather than a response in most of all 47 participants.

The same study demonstrated precursor recruitment and maturation toward broadly neutralizing antibody features. Among the VRC01-class monoclonal antibodies examined in the reported analysis, 39% neutralized the fully glycosylated tier-2 pseudovirus BG505.T332N, although weakly. Additional neutralization of heterologous viruses was reported, particularly for viruses naturally lacking the N276 glycan. These are isolated-antibody and pseudovirus findings, not a demonstration of vaccine-mediated protection against HIV. The supplied review used a substantive XML extraction containing results and methods, truncated during the references; separate supplementary material and figure images were not inspected.

CIDRAP's September 29, 2026 universal-influenza vaccine landscape update describes investigational approaches, including a newly registered phase 1 chimeric-hemagglutinin mRNA trial. It separately reports FDA approval of seasonal mRNA-1010, also called mFlusiva. That seasonal-vaccine approval should not be interpreted as approval of a universal influenza vaccine. The update documents particular developments and is not a comprehensive search establishing the absence of broader efficacy results.

On February 3, 2026, UW Medicine reported that GBP511, a pan-sarbecovirus nanoparticle vaccine, had begun a phase 1/2 trial in Australia, with enrollment starting the previous month in Perth. The announcement reported that preclinical studies protected animals against related viruses they had not been directly immunized against. The human trial was evaluating safety and immune responses, with results expected by 2028. That date was a projection, and the reported animal protection does not establish human efficacy or protection across all coronaviruses.

Two additional research-note assertions remain unverified in the supplied evidence. A claimed November 1, 2026 HIV review, identified as DOI 10.1097/COH.0000000000001070, was not supplied, and its author list was not retrieved because the PubMed page would not load. Its statements about several induced precursor classes and a need for two or three specificities therefore cannot be confirmed here. The notes also describe a 39-person phase 1 DNA pan-sarbecovirus vaccine trial as tolerable, with modest immune responses amid substantial pre-existing immunity, citing DOI 10.1016/j.jinf.2026.106759; no source document for that trial was supplied. These assertions remain possible findings requiring verification, rather than established results in this record.

The retained evidence does not demonstrate the proposed broad human protection against HIV, protection sustained across multiple years of influenza mismatch, or human protection against a zoonotic coronavirus absent from the vaccine. However, the supplied search record contains no bounded freshness searches, so it cannot substantiate the earlier statement that no such result had been found as of November 1, 2026. The supported conclusion concerns what these supplied materials demonstrate, not whether additional results existed elsewhere.

completion_criteria.text: NIAID's February 28, 2018 release provides a published external benchmark for universal influenza vaccination: at least 75% effectiveness, protection against influenza A groups 1 and 2, protection for at least one year, and suitability for all ages. The supplied release does not specify symptomatic influenza as the efficacy endpoint. These criteria are an influenza-specific benchmark, not an established completion standard for family-wide vaccines against every virus.
completion_criteria.label: Influenza protection meets NIAID’s full benchmark, including ≥75% effectiveness

completion_criteria.text: Proposed primary demonstration: show durable human protection across substantial, explicitly characterized antigenic diversity in one highly variable viral target. A convincing study would define the clinical endpoint, effect threshold, follow-up period and populations in advance, using the influenza benchmark where appropriate. It would distinguish protection against infection, symptomatic disease and severe disease, and establish which outcome the vaccine actually achieves. Precursor frequencies, selected monoclonal-antibody activity and neutralizing titers against a vaccine-matched virus alone would not satisfy this proposed protection criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Durable human protection spans substantial, explicitly characterized antigenic diversity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and escape demonstration: evaluate protection across diverse circulating viruses and, where feasible, prospectively encountered variants or relatives whose exact surface proteins were absent from the vaccine. Complement clinical outcomes with laboratory characterization of neutralization, target-site coverage and breakthrough viruses. Such tests would establish breadth across the viruses and conditions examined; finite testing cannot establish literal coverage of all future variants or unseen relatives.
completion_criteria.label: Protection breadth and escape are characterized across diverse viruses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed generality demonstration: apply the same underlying design logic to a second viral family and obtain protection, including against a virus whose exact surface protein was not a vaccine antigen. Animal protection would provide an intermediate demonstration of transfer. Human protection in the second family would provide stronger evidence for the intended human capability. The experimental setting and taxonomic scope should be explicit, and success in two families should not be presented as universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Design transfer protects against vaccine-unrepresented viruses in another family

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the protective findings in independent studies and characterize performance across relevant ages, prior infection or vaccination histories, and follow-up periods. Establish a usable immunization schedule, acceptable safety, reproducible vaccine production and any need for later boosting or antigen updates. These are proposed conditions for convincing and practical completion, rather than thresholds already established by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce protection and establish practical vaccination boundaries

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with VIR-01, “A prospective sequence-to-phenotype theory of infectivity, transmission, and escape”: predictive understanding of escape could help select antigens and stress-test expected coverage. VIR-01 concerns predicting viral properties from sequence; VIR-04 requires inducing and demonstrating protective immunity. Neither capability alone establishes the other.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-05, “Durable immunity at the respiratory surface that stops transmission”: antigenic breadth and protection at the respiratory surface are complementary properties. A vaccine could protect against diverse viruses while incompletely blocking infection at the mucosa, or produce strong mucosal protection against a narrower set. VIR-04 therefore does not subsume the transmission-blocking capability described by VIR-05.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-09, “A mechanistic correlate that predicts human protection from a new virus”: a validated correlate could help interpret immune measurements and potentially accelerate evaluation, but prediction of protection is distinct from creating broad protection. The roster identifies VIR-09 with the predictive correlate; the supplied material does not establish deployment speed as an independent completion requirement for that entry.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-11, “An interruptible causal chain from a persistent virus to a major chronic disease”: preventing a causal infection could interrupt later disease without requiring family-wide immunity. The research notes' proposed example of preventing multiple sclerosis through Epstein–Barr virus prevention illustrates that distinction, but the supplied sources do not establish that specific causal or intervention claim. VIR-11 remains a separate capability concerning interruption of a virus-to-disease pathway.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-02, “Empiric medicines that cover the major causes of severe acute viral disease,” VIR-03, “Scalable elimination or permanent silencing of persistent viral genomes,” and VIR-10, “A single-dose, conditionally replicating interfering particle that keeps a chronic virus suppressed”: these entries concern treatment, removal, silencing or sustained suppression of infection. VIR-04 concerns protective immune breadth. These approaches could complement vaccination, especially where prevention is incomplete, while retaining distinct mechanisms and outcome requirements.

Conceptual comparison with VIR-08, “A general experimental reading of viral genes that have no recognizable relatives”: interpreting unfamiliar viral genes could inform discovery of targets or mechanisms, but does not itself demonstrate broad protective immunity. VIR-06, “Bacteriophage therapy that can be prescribed as reliably as an antibacterial drug,” and VIR-07, “Viral particles that can be aimed at chosen human cells, given again, and carry large genes,” concern therapeutic use of viruses or viral particles. Their shared virology does not make them instances of VIR-04. These comparisons are based on the supplied roster titles, not full records for the other concepts.

change_log.change: Preserved VIR-04's identity while making family-wide and future-relative protection an intended, empirically bounded capability.
change_log.reason: Conserved-site targeting and finite demonstrations do not establish protection against every future virus.

change_log.change: Integrated precursor recruitment, directed maturation, glycan barriers, potency, durability and multiple-target escape reasoning into the concept and missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: The research and review together explain why human priming is meaningful progress but does not complete protective vaccination.

change_log.change: Corrected the GT1.1 paper date to 2025 as reported in the retained document and clarified enrollment and response denominators.
change_log.reason: The 47 participants included eight placebo recipients; documented responses were 11/18 low-dose and 13/19 high-dose evaluable recipients.

change_log.change: Preserved the 39% isolated-antibody neutralization result with weak potency, glycan dependence and assay scope.
change_log.reason: The quantitative finding supports maturation progress without establishing broad serum neutralization or human protection.

change_log.change: Retained the missing HIV review and 39-person DNA vaccine trial as explicitly unverified research-note assertions.
change_log.reason: Their source documents were absent; that limits verification without proving the assertions false.

change_log.change: Corrected the NIAID benchmark to effectiveness, influenza A group coverage, one-year duration and suitability for all ages, without attributing a symptomatic-disease endpoint.
change_log.reason: Those are the criteria supported by the supplied release; the precise clinical endpoint was not established there.

change_log.change: Separated seasonal influenza vaccine approval, investigational universal-influenza approaches, reported GBP511 animal protection and projected human trial results.
change_log.reason: These findings concern different products, stages and outcomes and cannot be combined into a completed broad human vaccine capability.

change_log.change: Distinguished sarbecovirus breadth from protection across the entire coronavirus family and excluded MERS-CoV from the sarbecovirus grouping.
change_log.reason: The review identified a taxonomic error in the UW article that should not be propagated.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical no-result-found statement with a conclusion limited to the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: No bounded freshness search record was supplied to establish the complete state of research in November 2026.

change_log.change: Made second-family transfer, clinical outcomes, reproducibility and practical boundaries explicit proposed demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Animal and human protection establish different levels of generality, and proposed thresholds should not be presented as established standards.

change_log.change: Expanded roster comparisons while distinguishing title-based conceptual reasoning from documented relationships.
change_log.reason: Only roster titles were supplied for the other entries; their full contents and the EBV–multiple sclerosis example were not independently supported.

unresolved_issues: The November 1, 2026 HIV review was not supplied. Its attribution, several-precursor-class statement and proposed two-or-three-specificity requirement remain unverified.

The claimed 39-person DNA pan-sarbecovirus trial lacks a supplied source document; its enrollment, tolerability, immune-response findings and interpretation of pre-existing immunity remain unverified.
The GT1.1 source was partially extracted, with truncation during references; separate supplementary material and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review.
The supplied release does not establish the clinical endpoint underlying NIAID's 75% effectiveness benchmark.
The completion proposal still requires target-specific choices of clinical endpoint, protective effect, duration, population coverage and the viral diversity considered sufficient.
Whether second-family completion should require human protection, or accept animal protection as an intermediate milestone, remains a proposed framework choice rather than an established resolution.
No bounded freshness search record establishes whether additional qualifying human efficacy results existed by November 1, 2026.
The EBV–multiple sclerosis example and the full scopes of the related roster entries remain undocumented beyond the supplied notes and titles.

brief.title: Vaccines that protect against a virus and its relatives
possible: People could receive vaccines that keep protecting them as viruses change, including against related viruses absent from the vaccine. The approach would train immunity to recognize vulnerable features shared across diverse viruses.
Vaccine developers could prepare protection against some animal viruses before they cause human outbreaks. The goal is a design method that works across different viral families.
why: Flu vaccines are rebuilt each year to match expected strains. Broader, lasting protection would reduce dependence on getting that match right and keep vaccination useful against a wider range of circulating viruses.
A reusable design method would give vaccine developers a way to prepare for related threats together, rather than waiting for each virus to emerge.

sources.who: Anthony S. Fauci and colleagues at NIAID
sources.showed: They set a benchmark and research strategy for flu vaccines that protect broadly and durably across ages.
sources.cited_for: The benchmark defines what a broadly protective flu vaccine should achieve.
sources.not_established: A research strategy does not demonstrate a vaccine that meets its benchmark.

sources.showed: In a small human HIV vaccine trial, they activated rare immune cells capable of developing antibodies that block diverse viruses. Some isolated antibodies blocked laboratory stand-ins for HIV.
sources.quote: A subset of isolated VRC01-class monoclonal antibodies neutralized wild-type pseudoviruses and was structurally extremely similar to bnAb VRC01.
sources.cited_for: Vaccination can start immune responses with features needed for broad HIV protection.
sources.not_established: The trial did not demonstrate broad, durable protection against HIV in people.

sources.showed: Their update described experimental flu vaccines, including early human testing and animal results. It separately reported approval of a seasonal flu vaccine.
sources.quote: elicited protective immunity against influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV infection in mouse, ferret, and cotton rat models
sources.cited_for: Broader flu vaccine approaches are being tested.
sources.not_established: The developments described do not establish lasting human protection across diverse flu viruses.

sources.who: UW Medicine researchers and SK bioscience
sources.showed: Their GBP511 vaccine protected animals against related viruses absent from the vaccine and entered human testing. It targets sarbecoviruses, a subgroup of coronaviruses.
sources.quote: In preclinical studies, GBP511 protected animals from related viruses they weren’t directly immunized against.
sources.cited_for: Animal studies demonstrate protection against relatives absent from a vaccine.
sources.not_established: Animal protection does not establish human protection or coverage of the entire coronavirus family.

shown: Caniels and colleagues have shown that an HIV vaccine can recruit rare immune cells and move them toward making antibodies that block diverse viruses. Some isolated antibodies blocked laboratory test viruses, but activity against a virus with its full protective sugar coating was weak.

UW Medicine researchers reported that GBP511 protected animals against related viruses absent from the vaccine. Human testing began to assess safety and immune responses. Its underlying animal work was described in a preprint, a paper awaiting peer review.
missing: Vaccination still needs to produce immune responses broad, strong and lasting enough to protect people across substantial viral diversity.
Follow-up doses still need to turn promising early immune cells into reliably protective responses.
A shared design method still needs to deliver protection against relatives absent from a vaccine in another viral family.
Independent studies still need to establish reproducible protection and a practical vaccination schedule.

milestones.label: Flu protection meets the full benchmark
milestones.explanation: A vaccine would have to meet NIAID’s benchmark: at least 75% effectiveness, coverage of both influenza A groups, annual protection and suitability for all ages. This sets the flu-specific standard.

milestones.label: Lasting human protection spans clearly defined viral diversity
milestones.explanation: A human study would have to show lasting protection across substantial, clearly described viral diversity using predefined measures. This would establish protection beyond promising laboratory responses.

milestones.label: Testing defines coverage and routes around immunity
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to measure protection across diverse viruses and examine viruses that evade immunity, including new relatives where feasible. This would define the demonstrated reach and limits of protection.

milestones.label: The design protects against relatives in another viral family
milestones.explanation: The same design logic would have to protect against a virus absent from the vaccine in another family. Animal protection would be an intermediate result; human protection would strengthen the case for reuse.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce protection and establish practical use
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce protection across relevant ages and immune histories, with acceptable safety, reliable production and a usable schedule. This would establish practical vaccination boundaries.

uncertain: How much viral diversity, protection and follow-up would be enough to count as success for each target?
Which combination of shared viral targets would best limit escape from immunity?
Would animal protection in another viral family suffice as an intermediate result, or should completion require human protection?

page.title: Broadly protective antiviral vaccines
page.definition: Vaccines protect people against antigenically diverse members of a defined viral group, including viruses whose antigens—components recognised by the immune system—were absent from the vaccine. Protection has a specified clinical endpoint, population and duration.

goal.need: WHO recommends annual influenza vaccination and issues vaccine-composition recommendations twice yearly for the northern and southern hemispheres. Current vaccines are routinely updated to match circulating viruses; this requires repeated strain selection alongside the annual disease burden shown below.

figures.caption: Estimated annual global burden of seasonal influenza
figures.note: These are burden estimates, not estimates of cases preventable by a universal vaccine.

statements.body: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
statements.quote: vaccines that are more broadly and durably protective are needed.
statements.context: The strategic plan addresses seasonal and pandemic influenza.

statements.quote: Activity against other coronaviruses (including other sarbecoviruses) and/ or potential future variants is highly preferred.
statements.context: Preferred indication in WHO's COVID-19 vaccine target product profile.

statements.quote: Developing a universal sarbecovirus vaccine is a critical challenge that must be addressed to prepare for the next pandemic.
statements.context: Chief executive Jaeyong Ahn's statement accompanying initiation of the GBP511 phase 1/2 trial on 29 January 2026.

statements.body: NIAID Vaccine Research Center and the GT1.1 vaccine trial consortium
statements.quote: A protective HIV vaccine will need to induce broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in humans
statements.context: The opening statement of the consortium's human vaccine trial report; these antibodies inhibit diverse HIV variants.

completion.title: A regulator licenses a vaccine with an explicit indication spanning a defined viral group.
completion.criterion: A national regulator licenses a vaccine covering multiple HIV-1 clades, influenza A groups 1 and 2, or sarbecoviruses beyond SARS-CoV-2. Accepted human evidence establishes protection against antigenically distinct members absent from the vaccine's antigens; the indication specifies population, endpoint and duration. For influenza, also require NIAID's ≥75% protection against symptomatic influenza, both influenza A groups, ≥1 year and suitability for all ages. The authorised breadth delimits completion; protection against every future relative is not established.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no common cross-target completion criterion was located. Regulatory licensure is the external decision, but the breadth condition here is an Atlas choice.
completion.basis: Searches of NIAID's influenza criteria, WHO product profiles and vaccine-evaluation guidelines, FDA licensure guidance and CIDRAP's coronavirus roadmap found no shared breadth/duration test or two-family transfer rule. The fallback uses one licensed cross-protection claim, bounded by its indication. FDA evaluates safety, effectiveness and manufacturing quality; CIDRAP explicitly calls for clarification of regulatory breadth.

milestones.title: A candidate vaccine elicits animal immunity and is judged safe enough for human testing.
milestones.criterion: Relevant animal immunogenicity and toxicity findings support human testing. WHO generally regards one relevant animal species as sufficient for toxicity assessment and calls for the intended clinical administration route. On 3 February 2026, UW Medicine reported GBP511 animal protection against related viruses absent from the vaccine. That evidence was described in a preprint, not peer reviewed; the announcement gives no animal group sizes and does not establish the full safety package.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, nonclinical vaccine guidelines, sections 3 and 4.1; a general vaccine-development criterion.

milestones.title: A candidate vaccine is administered to its first participant under an authorised human-study protocol.
milestones.criterion: The first participant receives vaccine in a permitted clinical investigation. In the United States, the IND takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt without a clinical hold, or on earlier FDA permission; investigator and ethics requirements also apply. The GT1.1 report of 31 July 2025 describes 47 adults and recruitment of antibody-producing cell precursors, without a protective-efficacy test. The pEVAC-PS phase 1 paper published on 18 May 2026 reports 39 adults aged 18–50 receiving two doses 28 days apart, with tolerability and modest immune responses.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, 21 CFR 312.40; the 30-day rule is US-specific, and other jurisdictions require their own clinical-trial permission.
milestones.threshold_quote: may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect

milestones.title: Human safety and immune responses support selection of a vaccine formulation for pivotal testing.
milestones.criterion: Safety and immunogenicity in the intended target population support selection of antigen dose, adjuvant and formulation for pivotal evaluation. WHO does not prescribe one numerical acceptance value for all vaccines. In the FLU-v phase IIb study published on 13 March 2020, 153 adults aged 18–55 were randomised and 123 underwent H1N1 challenge. Mild-to-moderate influenza occurred in 13/40 single-dose recipients versus 23/42 placebo recipients, with one-sided p=0.035. This tested one challenge strain.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, clinical vaccine-evaluation guidelines, section 4.2.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: sufficient safety and immunogenicity data to support the selection

milestones.title: A vaccine meets the efficacy criterion for its proposed breadth in a pivotal human trial.
milestones.criterion: A pivotal trial supports the proposed protection claim. Against an unvaccinated control, the lower 95% confidence bound for efficacy exceeds a prespecified clinically important percentage above zero. Active-control trials meet a justified prespecified non-inferiority margin. Endpoint, population, breadth and follow-up are protocol-specific. On 23 October 2020, BiondVax reported that M-001 missed primary and secondary efficacy endpoints in 12,463 adults aged ≥50, followed for one influenza season each; the primary safety endpoint was met. This company report was not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, clinical vaccine-evaluation guidelines, sections 4.2.2, 6.3.9.3 and 6.3.9.5.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: efficacy is above a predefined percentage (which will always be above zero).

not_found: No common numerical breadth/duration threshold or requirement for transfer between viral families was found in the NIAID, WHO, FDA and CIDRAP documents searched.
The GBP511 preclinical preprint could not be opened, and the UW announcement does not give animal group sizes.
The full GT1.1 article and supplements could not be reopened; its abstract and figure captions were accessible through PubMed.
The WHO influenza preferred-product-characteristics revision published on 4 December 2025 was located, but its PDF could not be opened.
A newsletter claim of a Chinese universal-influenza vaccine approval could not be matched to an NMPA decision or a primary efficacy report.
